Bid choosers with many bids

Your Bridge pick taken to the games with many bids: one chooser over one row of buttons, both the same width, the white card on the picked bid, no lines, square cells and the lowest bid you can make picked at the start. Spades and Twenty-Nine have fourteen bids, Double Deck Pinochle 49 and Pinochle 76. Each version is a way to hold that many. Tap the bids to try them. Every piece is drawn by the site’s own stylesheet.

What changes for the player

Today a tap on a bid sends it at once. With a chooser the lowest bid you can make is picked at the start, so the usual bid, one over the last, is still one tap: the button. Any other bid is two taps, the bid and then the button, and the button shows the bid before it goes.

Spades has no Pass, so its row is your bid alone. Its lowest bid is Nil, which carries its own rules, so a Spades chooser starts on 1.

Two rows of seven show fourteen bids, so Spades and Twenty-Nine need no arrows. Pinochle needs six pages and Double Deck four. Each page starts at the lowest bid you can make, so a bid you cannot make is only shown near the top.

The sliders

A slider alone is too coarse for this many bids. Pinochle’s 76 bids leave about 3px a bid on a desktop and 2px on a phone. A touch can land about 4mm off, which is about twelve bids on a phone. The finger also hides the card, and it nudges the card as it lifts. The design systems we read agree that a slider suits rough values. An exact value needs a step beside it (Apple, Microsoft, Material, Nielsen Norman Group). Poker apps put quick bets and small steps beside their sliders. No rival Pinochle app uses a slider. NeuralPlay and KARMAN show the bid between a minus and a plus. All three Pinochle apps we looked at open on the lowest bid.

Version 4 is the usual slider. It acts as sliders do in a desktop browser and on Android. While you drag, the bid shows in our own tooltip, as Material’s slider shows its value in Material’s own tooltip. Version 5 adds one-bid steps on a tap beside the card. Version 6 is version 4 with more room for the low bids, since most bids are low. Version 7 is a ruler, as in the iPhone photo editor. Versions 4 to 6 ignore the nudge as the finger lifts.

Desktop and phone

Sliders look and act the same on both. The difference is the hand. A finger hides the card, so the tooltip matters most on a phone. A finger also needs a touch area of 44px (Apple) or 48px (Material), so the slider takes a touch a little above and below its edge. A desktop adds the keyboard’s ← and → keys. A tap on the rail jumps there in a desktop browser and on Android. On an iPhone, Safari’s own slider ignores that tap. Our slider jumps there everywhere. A mouse can hit a bid 3px wide, but a finger cannot hit one 2px wide.

So I would build one slider for both, version 6. The keys only work where there is a keyboard, and the bigger touch area costs a desktop nothing. Material’s slider is also one slider for touch, mouse and keys.

The bid to beat

The bid to beat already shows on the bidder’s plate, as KARMAN’s Pinochle shows a bid under the name. The slider starts on the lowest bid you can make, and the yellow button names it. So I would add nothing (example A). The chooser needs no question in the notice either, since its buttons say what to do. The notice could say the bid to beat in words (B), but that only repeats the plate. The top bid only matters if you drag to the end, where the tooltip shows it. Both ends on the slider (C) take about a third of its room on a phone.

Questions for you

  • Which version? Two rows of seven, one row of seven, the stepper or one of the sliders? It can differ by game.
  • Should the low bids get more room? Version 6 gives the ten bids above the lowest half the chooser. The bids more than ten over then get less room than in version 4.
  • Does the bid to beat need more than the plate? Example B puts it in the notice, and C puts it on the slider with the top bid.
  • Should a tap beside the card step one bid? Version 5 does this. It makes every bid easy to reach on a phone, but a tap then acts in a less usual way.
  • Where do the arrows go? Here they sit in the row of buttons, where today’s Pinochle box has them. They could also be cells at the ends of the chooser.
  • What should be picked at the start? The lowest bid you can make, or the hint’s bid, the one the game’s own bot would make?

How it would be built

For the redesign only. The chooser is the suit pill’s paper with number cells (the Bridge chooser’s word cells, built on 2 Oct), one mark and, for two rows, a mark that moves between them. The stepper is the same pill with an arrow cell at each end, drawn as the pill draws a suit. A slider is the pill’s paper with a rail in the tray line and the white card on it. The bid shows in the site’s tooltip, #wtip from FrontpageTooltip.js. It opens on a hover or a tap today, so it needs one more call that keeps it over a moving card. The pager in the row of buttons is today’s back and forth button on the felt. The proposal rules are at the bottom of chooser-lab-parts/lab.css. In the code it touches each game’s showBid and the bid spots in its layout.
